question: Would offering flexible start times across all 30 depots reduce voluntary staff turnover?
purpose: Decide whether to roll out flexible start times to all 30 depots.

inclusion: Reports voluntary turnover, or intention to leave, for staff with and without flexible start times
Distribution, warehouse or comparable shift-based work
exclusion: Coverage of a source already included that adds no data
protocol.synthesis_method: Narrative synthesis with a structured summary of effects
assumptions: 'Turnover' means voluntary leavers as a share of staff in post
The five supplied documents are everything available; no search was run

sources.title: Northfield Logistics: Flexible Start Pilot, Final Report

concerns: Only 12 clusters and the analysis did not adjust for clustering, so the interval is too narrow
Two of six flexible depots opened canteens during the pilot
Evaluated by the employer's own team

sources.context: 12 depots, 1,184 staff (602 flexible, 582 fixed), twelve months

sources.title: Flexible starts slash staff turnover by a quarter
sources.exclusion_reason: Coverage of S1 that adds no data; its 'quarter' is S1's 4-point difference restated as a relative change

sources.title: Shift flexibility and intention to leave: a cross-sectional survey

concerns: Measures intention to leave, not leaving
Cross-sectional: cannot show that flexibility causes the difference

sources.title: Customer story: how ShiftWise cut turnover by 40% at Calder Freight

concerns: Published by the vendor of the rostering product to generate sales
No comparison group and no method stated
Pay rose 9% and the night shift closed in the same year

sources.title: Flexible start times in distribution: an 18-month matched evaluation
sources.design: Matched comparison, 9 flexible and 9 matched depots

concerns: Depots were not randomly assigned; matched on region, size, pay band and prior turnover
Comparison depots belong to other employers

sources.context: 18 depots, 2,046 staff, 18 months, payroll outcomes, independently funded

claims.statement: Flexible start times may reduce voluntary turnover by a few percentage points in the first six to twelve months.

support.text: Twelve-month voluntary turnover 13.0% (78 of 602) with flexible starts against 17.0% (99 of 582) with fixed starts; difference 4.0 percentage points (95% CI 0.0 to 8.1), p = 0.05
Turnover 6.1% in flexible depots against 8.4% in matched depots; difference -2.3 points (95% CI -4.6 to 0.0)
Voluntary turnover fell from 25% to 15% in a year at one employer, in the same year as a 9% pay rise and the closure of the night shift

claims.rationale: Two independent studies agree in direction, but both intervals reach zero, the randomised pilot did not adjust for clustering and had a co-intervention, and the other study was not randomised.
claims.conditions: Depot and warehouse staff; effect measured within the first year

claims.statement: The reduction may not last: the only evidence beyond twelve months found no difference in turnover from month 7 to month 18.

support.text: Turnover 14.9% in flexible depots against 14.2% in matched depots; difference +0.7 points (95% CI -2.4 to 3.8)

contradicts.text: A 4.0-point lower turnover over the full twelve months
contradicts.reconciled: S1 reports cumulative turnover for months 1 to 12 and does not separate early from late months, so it is compatible with an early reduction that fades.

claims.rationale: A single non-randomised study; its interval is compatible with a small lasting benefit or a small harm.

claims.statement: It is unclear whether any benefit is concentrated among staff in their first year.

support.text: Under one year's tenure: 21.4% turnover with flexible starts against 31.9% with fixed; one year or more: 9.8% against 10.6%. The tenure analysis was not planned in advance.

contradicts.text: Managers at five of the nine flexible depots said popular start slots filled quickly and newer staff were usually left with the least popular ones
contradicts.reconciled: unexplained: S1 finds the largest difference among new staff while S5 reports that new staff got the least choice; neither study tests this.

claims.rationale: One unplanned subgroup analysis in one pilot, in tension with managers' accounts in the other study.

claims.statement: Staff with some control over their start time are less likely to say they intend to leave, which shows an association with intention and not an effect on leaving.

support.text: Odds ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.87) for intending to leave within a year, adjusted for age, tenure and pay band; 2,310 staff, 22% response rate

claims.rationale: One cross-sectional survey read only as an abstract, with a low response rate.

claims.statement: If the early reduction fades, one possible reason is that popular start slots fill up and newer staff are left with little real choice.

support.text: Managers at five of the nine flexible depots said popular start slots filled quickly and newer staff were usually left with the least popular ones

claims.rationale: A mechanism suggested by managers' accounts in one study; not tested.

claims.statement: Do not roll out to all 30 depots on this evidence. Extend flexible starts to a randomly chosen subset of depots and track payroll turnover for at least 18 months before deciding.
claims.rationale: A possible short-term benefit of uncertain durability does not justify a full roll-out, but is enough to justify a test that would settle it.
